#136. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”

This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

#134. Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’

Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit

The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy’s longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits.

Kennedy and his allies have also profited from growing misinformation peddled through books, paid speaking events and the supplement industry.

“I do think he’s a real ideologue – he really believes in this,” said Dorit Reiss, professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. But Kennedy and his allies are likely “very happy to make money doing it”, she said.

Peter Hotez, professor and dean of Baylor College of Medicine’s National School of Tropical Medicine, agreed, saying Kennedy’s actions are likely a combination of “being an ideological zealot and making money either for himself or for his associates”.

Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said the department “categorically reject claims that Secretary Kennedy is pursuing personal gain or seeking to dismantle American medicine”.

Prior to his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy disclosed $2.5m in income from referrals for vaccine-related lawsuits. In the hearing, Kennedy would not commit to forgoing compensation from vaccine lawsuits after he leaves office. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, listed several ways in which Kennedy’s actions, some of which have now happened, could influence future litigation.

“Kennedy can kill off access to vaccines and make millions of dollars while he does it,” Warren said at the hearing. “Kids might die. But Robert Kennedy can keep cashing in.” She pointed to Kennedy’s involvement in litigation against Merck for its HPV vaccine – lawsuits that were settled for more than $50m in June 2026. After the confirmation hearing, Kennedy said his son would receive the money, expected to be 10% of the total; it’s unclear if he did.

“For most of us, money going to our children isn’t exactly money not going to us,” Reiss said. “There’s a dozen ways he and his family could benefit” from Kennedy’s actions, she added.

Kennedy has long profited from his anti-vaccine misinformation. Tony Lyons, Kennedy’s publisher and a central figure in the constellation of Maha political organizations, reportedly paid Kennedy $4m in book advances over the past year. The publisher also paid Kennedy $451,000 in consulting fees before he became HHS secretary. That’s on top of other book sales and paid speaking engagements over the years. Kennedy also earned $326,000 for the 15 weeks he served as chairman of Children’s Health Defense in 2023 – more than half of his $510,000 salary in 2022.

More recently, he received free flights and trips on a yacht from a former donor to his presidential campaign, who is now under investigation by the Senate for the gifts totaling some $250,000.

As HHS secretary, Kennedy has also loosened regulations on peptides, a booming part of the largely unregulated wellness industry.

“I think he’s doing what everyone knew he was going to do,” said Hotez. Kennedy, before and during his tenure as leader of HHS, has been “chipping away at public confidence in vaccines and immunizations in favor of products that can be sold by the wellness industry”, he added.

Aaron Siri, Kennedy’s former lawyer who represents people who say they have experienced severe side effects, has advocated for changing all vaccines to “shared clinical decision-making”. If those changes took place, Siri could argue that the vaccines are not covered under the VICP and therefore open to litigation.

“A lot of what he is doing is geared toward setting up a more profitable litigation atmosphere,” Reiss said.

Siri did not respond to the Guardian’s question about profiting from litigation, but instead argued that “if vaccines are as ‘safe’ as touted by the government, then there should be no need for immunity to liability and, likewise, there should be very few, if any, successful cases”.

The most common claim to VICP – making up more than half – has to do with where the vaccine is administered, not the vaccines themselves.

The VICP was established in 1986 in order to expedite compensation for anyone who experienced adverse side effects from vaccines. There are real costs to undermining the program, Reiss said. It’s very rare for people to develop severe side effects after vaccination, but when they do, they should be compensated, she said. But if false claims about vaccine harms proliferate, they will obscure those with legitimate claims.

Filing a VICP claim is an easier process than winning a lawsuit, which takes time and effort and also demands a higher burden of proof.

“That’s why the whole vaccine injury system was set up,” Hotez said. “It was actually to the plaintiff’s benefit to get a faster judgment without having to show detailed evidence of proof.”

Without VICP, patients would need to pay lawyers a large chunk of their settlements, if their case moves through the courts at all, Reiss said: “The lack of contingency fee means they don’t have to pay 30% to 50% of their earnings through the lawyer.”

Compensating doctors for reporting side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) risks offering “the wrong incentives” to unscrupulous providers who could increase such activities to become a new revenue source, Reiss said.

The changes could “certainly” be used by organizations such as Children’s Health Defense to legitimize its work spreading misinformation “and convince donors and others that they should give them more money”, she added.

VAERS, alongside several other vaccine monitoring systems, works well to pick up signals of very rare side effects, such as myocarditis from initial mRNA Covid vaccines and thrombotic thrombocytopenia in the Johnson and Johnson Covid vaccine, Hotez noted. But it’s not built to prove links between vaccines and certain side effects, as vaccination opponents have attempted to do, he said.

“The VAERS system was never meant to show cause and effect,” Hotez said. “It’s like looking for signs of alien communication in outer space. You look at every little blip, and almost all of them have nothing, are not real. But you have to analyze them.”

Years ago, Hotez engaged Kennedy in a series of conversations about misinformation that autism spectrum disorder is related to vaccines. Hotez pointed to known environmental influences on autism, like the anti-seizure medication valproic acid. Kennedy “had no interest then; he has no interest now”, Hotez said. “Even back then, there was a heavy emphasis on being a plaintiff attorney and suing vaccine companies. So that’s his narrow interest, which has nothing to do with reality – and he’s still going by the same playbook.”

Kennedy has attacked medical journals and schools, and funding for medical research has fallen sharply under his leadership. Such actions appear intended to “completely wipe out American medicine as we know it in favor of this whole system of grifting and pseudoscience”, Hotez said.

Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.

The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center.

In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times.

Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”.

In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda.

Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”.

Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends.

“Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.”

Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.”

For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship.

Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters.

The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns.

In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.

Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”.

Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”.

Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order. In late September, a federal appeals court for the 11th circuit rejected a request from Trump and his lawyers to immediately lift sanctions that Williams imposed in response to the settlement Trump and the DoJ backed over the leak of his tax returns.

In its ruling, the appeals court denied a request by two Trump lawyers, Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein, to pause sanctions against them over their handling of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS. The court ruled the lawyers had not demonstrated they would succeed in challenging finding that they acted in bad faith.

In another legal blow for Trump, two restraining orders were issued in October by district judge Jennifer Rochon in New York to stop his use of public funds for financing campaign style ads after Campaign Legal Center Action representing Common Cause, along with Public Integrity Project Action and Democracy Forward sued.

In her second emergency order on 30 October, Judge Rochon ruled that three ads could no longer run using government funds on Instagram and two other sites since they were “purely partisan” .

One of the ads echoed Trump’s dubious claim that if Republicans maintained control of Congress, all Americans would receive $5,000. The three ads Rochon ordered removed were headlined “$5,000 to Americans” the “Cost of Socialism” and “Every Democrat Voted against No Tax on Tips”.

Shortly before Rochon’s first ruling, Trump in a Truth Social post on 5 October defended using government funds for the ads and blithely stated that tapping public funds was “rather standard”.

But with growing criticism, including from some Republicans, Trump announced he would pay for them himself from his political fundraising operation. The justice department also tried to forestall the first restraining order by asserting that “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow”.

Renata O’Donnell, a senior legal counsel with Campaign Legal Center who worked on the case, told the Guardian: “The Department of Homeland Security used $20m in taxpayer dollars to pay a private ad agency for airtime for government-created propaganda. This is blatantly illegal.”

O’Donnell added: “In direct violation of the law, White House staff, whose salaries are paid with taxpayer dollars, were creating propaganda, including ads that promised people $5,000 to vote Republican.”

In another pending legal battle that courts have yet to rule on, Democracy Defenders Fund filed a lawsuit with the San Francisco city attorney, the Washington Litigation Group and Platkin LLP to block a Trump financial gambit to offer special early access to his Truth Social posts to users who pay a fee as high as $100,000 per month to the parent company of Truth Social.

The lawsuit was filed in mid-September against Trump Media and Technology Group, which operates and owns Truth Social.

San Francisco city attorney David Chiu asked the San Francisco superior court to bar Trump Media from offering its new service, dubbed “Trump API”, or a similar one, plus provide monetary damages for violating the public trust and the state’s unfair competition law.

“Trump Media created a marketplace that enables insider trading, which Trump directly profits from,” Chiu said in a statement. “This scheme turns the public trust into private profit. It is corruption, plain and simple.”

A Trump Media spokesperson ridiculed the lawsuit when it was filed, charging that “the people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the leftwing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information”.

David Ogden, a senior counsel with DDF who has worked on the case, noted that “Congress made clear that the president, like any public servant, shouldn’t be permitted to profiteer off of special access to government information. It’s a violation of the public trust and it’s important that it be stopped.”

In the eyes of Barbara McQuade, former US attorney for eastern Michigan, who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, the different court rulings against Trump’s financial ploys reveal his penchant for “personal enrichment” and political ploys during his presidency.

“It seems that Trump has no shame about using his office for personal enrichment. We can’t count on his own conscience, ethics or advisers to check his worst instincts, but the courts have seen through his various schemes, from his slush fund to his use of taxpayer funds for political ads.”

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

Exclusive: Shepard Fairey says image will hold PM accountable over promise to get people off the streets

The “Hope” portrait of Barack Obama by the US street artist Shepard Fairey came to symbolise a historic 2008 presidential campaign, became one of the most ubiquitous and reproduced political portraits of modern times, and ended up in the Smithsonian.

Fairey’s latest work, of the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, may not elicit the same response but will, he hopes, deliver a hard-hitting message: one of a promise made.

The portrait, “Home”, captures Burnham in a red Big Issue tabard when, as Greater Manchester mayor, he sold copies with vendor Colin in 2023, and is the front cover of a new collectors’ edition of the magazine.

Designed exclusively for the Big Issue, it’s a reminder to the new prime minister of his pledge to tackle rough sleeping. From Monday, it will be sold on streets, and also be unveiled on the walls of the Saatchi Gallery in London as part of a six-month street culture exhibition, Beyond the Streets.

Fairey said: “The thread that runs through all my work is a push for justice. This portrait reminds us of the pledge Burnham made. Politicians often want people to forget to hold them accountable for the promises they’ve made. This is harder to do when a symbol of that promise is in thousands of people’s hands.”

The art work was created after the Big Issue approached Fairey, who said he was “overjoyed” that the portrait would be in the public sphere. “What I wanted to convey was simply warmth, and a reminder that he has actually been out on the streets promoting and selling the Big Issue, even before he was prime minister,” he said.

The magazine also carries an exclusive interview with Burnham. In it, the prime minister said: “I don’t think anyone should sleep rough in this country … I’m not going to be naive. I can offer people a route off the streets, but not everybody will take it.

“What I can say though is, I can ask every council as part of the funding we’ve given to provide an offer to everyone. And that’s what we’re confident of now …

“Big Issue knows better than anybody. You get a surge of sentiment around rough sleeping later in the year, for really good reasons, but when you hit the earlier months of the new year it falls away. What I’m saying is that public money won’t fall away. That’s the only way to do it. Stop-start is not fair to the organisations that are out there working with rough sleepers. This is a fixable problem and it’s about a national effort to fix it.”

#123. Trident nuclear submarine concludes record underwater deployment

HMS Vengeance’s seven-month patrol prompts concerns about slow pace of maintenance of ageing fleet and impact on crew

A Trident nuclear submarine has concluded a record seven-month deployment, returning to the Faslane naval base in Scotland, where its crew are expected to be greeted by senior members of the government.

HMS Vengeance began its patrol on 12 April and spent 217 days submerged before returning on Sunday, leaving the country when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street and Manchester United were third in the Premier League.

Its tour underwater surpasses the old 205-day record, set by HMS Vanguard, and has raised questions about the strains placed on sailors and the reliability of ageing submarines sent on the extended missions.

“Patrols are getting longer and longer,” said David Cullen, a nuclear expert with the Basic thinktank. “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world.”

The increase in the time spent at sea reflects the slow pace of submarine maintenance, prompting Labour to blame spending cuts implemented by the Conservatives, though naval chiefs insist there is a plan for improvement.

HMS Vengeance is one of four submarines responsible for carrying Britain’s Trident nuclear missiles. At all times a boat is at sea, so the UK could launch strikes even if Britain had already been destroyed in a nuclear war.

When the Vanguard class of submarines was brought into service in the 1990s, they were designed to carry three to four months of food for the crew of about 140, and deployments of more than 100 days were considered highly exceptional. Missions now start with tinned food crammed into corridors and other available spaces.

Each submarine has to keep its location secret so it cannot be targeted, meaning it also cannot be resupplied. The boats maintain radio silence and so the crew cannot message out on the long deployments, though they can receive news and other information.

Such is the length of the patrols that the return of a Trident submarine, known as a “day zero”, has become a political event. Starmer made an unannounced visit when the last patrol ended in April, praising the crew on their return.

There have been worries about the psychological impact of the patrols on the crew members, who have to spend seven months underwater in a boat 150 metres long, at a time when the Royal Navy is struggling to recruit new personnel.

Last week, the head of the Royal Navy, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for the Trident sailors, but added that the UK needed to “improve our submarine maintenance” to allow faster turnaround.

The submarine service, in line with the rest of the navy, has a “no touching rule” – prohibiting physical intimacy on board – though the service has had to contend with allegations of sexual abuse and harassment during deployments.

In October 2024, the then first sea lord was forced to issue an apology to women – who make up about 10% of the navy – who had suffered “misogyny, bullying and other unacceptable behaviours” in the submarine service.

The navy conducted an inquiry after a whistleblower, Sophie Brook, complained of a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” from male sailors. Reports of rape, physical and verbal abuse were examined in a heavily redacted report.

Trident submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities, and a letter from the prime minister to tell the captain how to proceed in the event it is determined the UK no longer exists after an all-out nuclear attack.

Such is the length of the boat’s patrol it will still be carrying Starmer’s letter, though the replacement submarine on rotation will have Andy Burnham’s instructions, written in longhand in the days after he took over at Downing Street.

In July, Labour announced a £26bn, 10-year plan to invest in Britain’s three main naval bases, at Faslane, the operational home of the Trident submarines, Devonport and Portsmouth, as part of a wider increase in defence spending.

However, the first of the replacements for the four Vanguard class submarines, HMS Dreadnought, is not expected to be ready until about 2032, meaning that the old boats have at least five more years to remain in service.

“The inherent risks of operating submarines are being pushed by them being run as they are. At the end of the submarines’ design life they should be run gently, not as hard as they are,” Cullen said.

#120. Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled plans to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

#119. ‘No such thing as a free lunch,’ says Milburn as he warns it will take a decade for UK benefits bill to come down

Author of major review into youth unemployment rejects ‘crude cuts’ to payments and downplays opposition to his proposals within Labour

Alan Milburn has said “there is no such thing as a free lunch”, in response to critics who believe the government should make tougher cuts to out-of-work benefits for young people.

The former health secretary will publish a major review on Tuesday, urging ministers to implement radical reforms to address the UK’s youth unemployment crisis, which has seen the number of young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) rise to about a million.

He told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme the government would have to be “candid with people”, and that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down and for the country to reach a “reasonable level” of youth unemployment as a result of his recommendations.

He also warned the additional investment in young people would cost billions of pounds over a 10-year period.

Milburn said it was impossible to “wave a magic wand” and fix the crisis sooner. “You can if you just do crude cuts,” he clarified. “But if you do crude cuts in benefits, all that happens is that young people show up somewhere else on the government ledger.”

Asked what he would say to critics such as the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, who has repeatedly called for benefits to be slashed over a short period of time, he said: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means.

“I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have 1 million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.”

The Labour government is expecting opposition to Milburn’s recommendations from its own MPs on the left of the party, who rebelled against Keir Starmer’s plans to reform welfare last summer.

Asked about the mood in the parliamentary party, the former cabinet minister said: “When I talk to Labour MPs about this, they know quite well that in their constituencies there are hundreds, sometimes thousands, of young people who are being doomed to a life on benefits.”

Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s.

It will recommend that some young people with disabilities should lose their ongoing personal independence payment (Pip), and instead be able to apply to local funds for short-term expenses and equipment.

While entitlement for those with the most severe needs will be protected, most under-25s will be no longer eligible for either Pip or the health element of universal credit and will instead get a new youth allowance paid at the standard universal credit rate.

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, acknowledged the overhaul would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets, suggesting government intervention to compel young people to work or train would be strengthened.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

He told the channel’s Sunday Morning programme that countries that had dealt with youth unemployment successfully, such as the Netherlands, had teams who “literally knock on your door” and offer young people options for training or work.

McFadden also appeared on Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, where he warned that some people would receive fewer benefits as a result of the proposals.

Asked whether he agreed with some under-25s losing out, he said this was necessary because the number of young people claiming Pip had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had gone up by 80%.

Asked whether he agreed with Milburn that young people should not be able to claim health-related benefits, McFadden said: “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work. You will actually get more than you will now.

“He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs. And for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work.

“But the status quo is important for this reason … If you’re 20 right now and you sign on to long-term sickness benefits, you’ve got more chance of marking your 30th birthday and still being on them than having a steady job in between.”

#116. Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.

From India to France, the implicit meritocratic bargain that underwrote stable societies by providing advancement to new generations is breaking down.

Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

#113. Christmas ‘dupes’: the cheaper gift versions proving a festive hit in the cost of living crisis

From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cut-price versions of high-end sellers have gone mainstream. But is it fair?

For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

Dupes are products that claim to offer a similar experience to a high-end item though do not claim to be that product. They were originally a Gen Z obsession but have become a mainstream shopping trend at a time of strained household finances.

“No matter what age you are, how much money you’ve got to spend, everyone wants to ‘luxe it up’ with a dupe,” says Catherine Shuttleworth, a retail consultant and chief executive of Savvy Marketing.

“The message is ‘why not be smart like me saving cash but still looking good’,” she says.

“In the case of homewares, a high street dupe of a luxury branded candle can look and smell just as good as the real thing, and will your visitors really notice that your table lamps are from B&M not the White Company?”

Dupe culture is being supercharged by social media, particularly TikTok. More than 30 million people across the UK now use TikTok each month, according to the company, with Gen-Z’ers admitting that seeing products sell out or go viral makes them more likely to buy them.

Data firm YPulse has been tracking consumer attitudes to dupes for several years and Tori D’Amico, managing content editor, says: “The idea that a dupe can be a true replacement for a luxury item is still prevalent. Dupes are not shameful or embarrassing to own. Young consumers brag online about finding a good deal and share it with the masses.”

YPulse’s most recent research found that 44% of UK 13- to 39-year-olds have bought a dupe in the past year. When asked, just over half (53%) of this age group agreed that “the quality of dupe/fake luxury items makes me less likely to want to purchase a real luxury item”.

Dupes are particularly prominent in the beauty world but are also found in other sectors including food, furniture, homeware and designer fashion.

US “dupe” retailer Quince, which sells upmarket products ranging from candles to cashmere sweaters, has just launched in the UK. Alongside each product on its website it suggests the saving you are making against more expensive brands. A £50 woman’s red cashmere jumper, for example, is pictured alongside graphics comparing it with jumpers from Cos and Reiss costing three times as much.

Fragrance, in particular, is a popular target. There are more than 50,000 videos on TikTok under the combined hashtag #perfumedupe and #perfumedupes, where influencers rate imitation fragrances against famous names and tell viewers where to find them.

With fragrances a sought-after Christmas gift the platform is awash with content extolling these cheaper scents. Instead of spending nearly £130 on Mugler’s Alien try Zara’s Violet Blossom for £15.99, suggests one. Or, if you can’t afford Le Labo’s Another 13, try Marks & Spencer’s Aura Ambrette, a snip at £22.50.

In TikTok Dupeland budget supermarket Aldi is lauded as a perfume house with its Lacura brand tipped to offer substitutes for high-end favourites ranging from Paradoxe to Flowerbomb and Baccarat Rouge – for £7 a bottle.

“These cut-price products are in focus right now as consumers look for cheaper alternatives in response to rising prices,” says Eric Mills from market research firm NielsenIQ. In a recent survey, 38% of UK consumers said that in the past 12 months they had switched to lower-priced brands to manage their shopping bills.

“The buyers of these brands are often thought of as only younger consumers, but while Gen Z are key spenders, it’s millennials who account for the greatest proportion of sales,” he adds.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

In a microcosm of what is likely happening elsewhere in the market, the number of people buying dupe fragrances online is up 17% in the past year which is ahead of the overall market.

With the continued adoption of AI tools, Mills says: “It’s easy to imagine dupes gaining further traction, as consumers can simply ask a chatbot for a cheaper alternative to their favourite luxury scent.”

With dupes copying well-known brands without pretending to be the real thing they occupy a space somewhere between authentic and fake. While consumers might love dupes, the targets are less enthusiastic.

Celebrity makeup artist Charlotte Tilbury, whose £350m fortune stems from the sale of her eponymous beauty empire to Spanish fragrance and fashion group Puig, recently told the BBC that “when you dupe, you dupe the consumer”.

“It is not Charlotte Tilbury … and it is not performing the way that my products do,” Tilbury says of cheaper imitations. “If I could do them for those prices I would.”

Charlotte Tilbury has had some success pushing back and, in 2019, brought a successful copyright case against Aldi over the designs on its Filmstar Bronze & Glow palette which the supermarket had copied.

Claire Breheny, partner and head of trade marks at Mathys & Squire suggests that business owners should be requesting that dupes be taken down from online platforms or social media. Brand owners “need to protect their packaging and get-up, not just their name.

“The risk for consumers is that similar packaging doesn’t guarantee similar quality, ingredients or performance – although a cheaper alternative isn’t necessarily always going to be inferior.”

With the cost of living crisis only making dupes more attractive to shoppers, Savvy Marketing’s Shuttleworth says that nearly 80% of shoppers its survey polled were happy to selectively spend more on treats and luxuries where they think it’s worth it.

“The challenge for top brands like Charlotte Tilbury, is that they need to be able to convince shoppers the quality difference is always worth paying for.”

#110. French minister under fire for Playboy magazine cover

French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.

Schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights. Schiappa, who is the current Minister for the Social Economy and French Associations, was photographed for the cover wearing a white dress.

Schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017. In this role, she successfully spearheaded a new sexual harassment law which allows for on the spot fines to be issued to men who catcall, harass or follow women on the street.

Her appearance has drawn criticism from political colleagues including French Prime Minister Elisabeth Borne.

Borne pulled up Schiappa over the cover, telling her it “wasn’t appropriate, especially during this period,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported Saturday, citing a source close to the prime minister.

France is currently in the throes of a political and social crisis triggered by French President Emmanuel Macron’s move to push ahead with controversial pension reforms despite widespread public opposition.

“We are in the middle of a social crisis, there is the issue of policing, there are people between life and death, and I have the impression of being behind a smoke screen,” Sandrine Rousseau, Green Party politician and fellow women’s rights activist, told BFMTV Friday.

France wracked by more pension protests amid rising violence on the streets

French politician, Jean Luc Mélenchon who came third in the 2022 presidential elections criticized both Schiappa’s appearance and the decision by French President Emmanuel Macron to give an interview to children’s magazine, Pif Gadget, this week.

“In a country where the President expresses himself in Pif and his minister in Playboy, the problem would be the opposition. France is going off the rails,” Mélenchon tweeted Saturday.

Schiappa responded to her critics in a tweet on Saturday, saying: “Defending the right of women to have control of their bodies, that’s everywhere and all the time. In France, women are free. With all due respect to the detractors and hypocrites.”

French Interior Minister, Gérald Darmanin came to Schiappa’s defense during an interview with French news channel CNews on Sunday calling her a “woman of character.”

“I wanted to say that Marlene Schiappa is a courageous female politician who has her character and who has her style which is not mine, but I respect,” he remarked.

#109. The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’

A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.

Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.

I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.

“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.

On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.

Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”

Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

#108. Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other

So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.

The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.

Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.

Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

#107. Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm

Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.

A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.

Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.

Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.

This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.

The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.

Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”

Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.

Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.

“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.

Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.

A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.

Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”

Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.

The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.

Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.

“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

This article was amended on 9 November 2026. An earlier version said the Vantara zoo covers 400 hectares; in fact, it is 1,400 hectares.

#106. The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

“It’s so much more than the four names that have been announced,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”

Glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

The Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

If all goes to plan, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton said via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already said delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

“I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

“We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”

She said the offer rendered her “speechless.”

“It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.
